reader.title: Lynching of a gambler in a Colorado mining town (1880)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A crowd of miners took a prisoner accused of killing a police officer from the town lock-up and hanged him (A23, A24); the July Kokomo dispatches describe a jail taken by a mob and a hanging (A2, A3).

Ramsey's account has fifteen or twenty men break into the 'cooler', hang the prisoner for killing an officer and tell him 'you got to swing for it' (A23, A24); the Kokomo dispatches likewise report a mob or crowd taking a prisoner from deputies and hanging him (A2, A3, A18).

The detailed account of 'Jim' comes from one eyewitness, Oil Inspector Ramsey, reprinted under two Pittsburgh credits (A23, A24); the Kokomo lynching of July 1880 is reported by several dispatches (A2, A3, A12) and closely matches it, but no paper says the two are the same event.

summary.text: The lynching of a gambler in a Colorado mining town was the hanging of a man called 'Jim', accused of shooting a police officer, by fifteen or twenty miners who took him from the town lock-up in 1880.
It is known chiefly from the account of a Pittsburgh oil inspector named Ramsey, who said he watched it, and whose story ran in eastern papers in late 1880.
His details closely match a lynching at Kokomo, near Leadville, reported in July 1880, though no paper said the two were the same.
According to the inquest testimony Ramsey recounted, two men quarreled over cards one evening in the gambling saloon of Jim Beggs.
When a police officer told them to make less noise, one of the gamblers was said to have drawn a revolver and shot him through the heart.
The accused man was held in the 'cooler', a frame station-house, under six guards.
The next morning a coroner's jury met over the officer's body, laid on two faro tables with a coiled rope and noose on top.
After the first witness spoke, a man in a red flannel shirt picked up the rope and walked out, followed by fifteen or twenty companions.
Finding that the guards had no keys, they broke the cooler door with an ax from a woodpile and brought the prisoner out with the noose around his neck.

The crowd led him to an old building with a beam over the sidewalk, where, Ramsey said, he offered $1,000 to be shot instead and was refused with 'You murdered a good man, and you got to swing for it.'
Hauled up, he grasped the rope above his head, so the men lowered him, tied his arms and raised him again, leaving him hanging for nearly an hour.
Afterward the 'committee' had a photographer take a picture of the group with the body behind them.
The dead man's companion was given six hours to leave town.
No report of arrests or prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

Ramsey's story first appeared in Pittsburgh and was reprinted by the Chicago Daily Tribune on November 29, 1880, credited to the Pittsburg Evening News, and by the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer on December 1, credited to the Pittsburgh Dispatch.

Both ran it as a frontier anecdote under the line 'Initiation of a Pittsburgh Gentleman into Western Mining Life', calling the victim 'the murderer' and placing 'committee' and 'gang' in quotation marks.
Neither printing named the town or the date or gave anyone's race.
The July Kokomo reports were brief wire items with headlines such as 'A Murderer Lynched' and 'Judge Lynch Metes Out Justice'.
The Topeka Tribune closed its item with the victim's reported admission that he had killed three other men 'and that the punishment was just.'
The July dispatches name the Kokomo victim as Charley or Chas. Norton, or as Charles Thompson, a saloon keeper, and the officer as Michael O'Neil.
A Leadville telegram printed in the New York Sun put the shooting at about 2 a.m. and the hanging from a tree outside town an hour later, while a Denver dispatch placed the shooting in the afternoon.
Ramsey, by contrast, described an evening shooting and a hanging in town the next morning, during the inquest.

accounts.label: Eyewitness (Ramsey)
accounts.gist: An officer was shot in Jim Beggs's saloon one evening; the next morning, during the inquest, fifteen or twenty miners took the gambler Jim from the cooler, hanged him from a beam over a sidewalk and had a photograph made.

accounts.label: Leadville telegram via Chicago
accounts.gist: Charley Norton shot Policeman O'Neil at Kokomo about 2 a.m.; a mob took him from the jail about an hour later and hanged him from a tree outside town after he confessed to three murders.

accounts.label: Denver dispatch
accounts.gist: Chas. Norton, drunk, shot O'Neil in the afternoon while resisting arrest; a crowd overpowered the deputies guarding him and lynched him.

accounts.label: Denver dispatch, July 25
accounts.gist: Saloon keeper Charles Thompson shot City Marshal Michael O'Neil on Friday night and was found asleep in another saloon; the rest is cut off.

framing.detail: Ramsey's story ran as a human-interest piece, 'A Colorado Lynching', calling the victim a 'murderer' and 'the poor devil' and putting 'committee' and 'gang' in quotation marks.
July headlines called it 'Judge Lynch Metes Out Justice' and 'A Murderer Lynched' and reported the victim's admission that the punishment was just.
The Denver dispatch ran nearly word for word in Washington and Cheyenne papers.

conflicts.note: Ramsey's account names no town or date; linking it to the Kokomo lynching rests on the close match of the details.

versions.value: Next morning, from a beam over a sidewalk in town, after an evening shooting
About 3 a.m., an hour after the shooting, from a tree a short distance from town

conflicts.note: The accounts disagree on timing; Ramsey's morning hanging during the inquest cannot be squared with the 3 a.m. telegram.
The two printings credit different Pittsburgh papers for the same text.

record_check.dossier: No report gives the race of the victim, the officer or the lynchers; nothing marks this as anti-Black violence
Undated by Ramsey ('several months ago'); if it is the Kokomo lynching, July 23, 1880 (dispatches disagree on the hour)
Unnamed by Ramsey; probably Kokomo, Colorado, near Leadville
Jim in Ramsey's account; Charley Norton or Charles Thompson in the July dispatches
Ramsey's story ran by 1880-11-29; the Kokomo dispatches ran from 1880-07-24

record_check.record: took the gambler Jim, who had shot a police officer
record_check.dossier: The shooting is an accusation recounted by an inquest witness and Ramsey, not an established fact

info: Not dated by Ramsey, who visited the West 'several months' before late November 1880
Probable match: Kokomo, Colorado, near Leadville, where a lynching for the killing of a policeman was reported on July 23, 1880
'Jim', a richly dressed gambler (Ramsey); Charley/Chas. Norton (A2, A3, A18) or Charles Thompson, a saloon keeper (A12) in the Kokomo dispatches; race not stated in any report
Accused of shooting dead a police officer who had told two quarreling gamblers in Jim Beggs's saloon to make less noise
Miners led by a man in a red flannel shirt; Ramsey calls them the 'committee'
No report of arrests, indictment or trial of the lynchers was found

acts.note: Man in red flannel shirt took up the rope from beside the dead officer and walked out followed by 15-20 men.
Guards had no keys; crowd broke the cooler door with an ax and took the prisoner out with the noose on his neck.
Leader refused $1,000 to be shot: 'you got to swing for it.'
Hanged from a beam; lowered when he grasped the rope, arms tied, hauled up again; hung nearly an hour.
Dead man's companion given six hours to leave town.
